description: we are building a space game.
summary:
We developed Unit-01: Project Horizon, a story-driven space exploration game that turns learning into a rescue mission. Players control a small utility robot exploring a fictional environment near Phobos, recovering supplies, studying samples, repairing equipment and helping an injured astronaut escape.
The project addresses the challenge of making space science engaging by connecting information to meaningful actions. Players investigate materials, recover exploration data and complete a Mars science quiz as they progress through the story.
Built with C++17 and an optional SDL2 graphical interface, Project Horizon combines exploration, problem-solving and an emotional narrative about cooperation and sacrifice. Its intended impact is to encourage curiosity about planetary science and robotics while helping players see how observation, engineering and careful decisions contribute to space exploration.
details:
Project Details
What it does and how it works
Project Horizon takes players between an explorable surface and a damaged ship containing storage, a cargo hangar, a monitor room and an engine room. As Unit-01, players recover medical supplies and food, examine silicate, water-ice and rock samples, repair a carrier robot, and scan a rescue spacecraft.
Learning is part of mission progression. Recovered data unlocks reading passages and nine multiple-choice questions about Mars, with opportunities to retry incorrect answers. Later missions involve gathering repair materials, escorting the injured astronaut and restoring the escape ship. The story ends with both robots transferring their remaining power to launch the astronaut to safety.
Benefits and intended impact
The game aims to make space science approachable through exploration and purposeful tasks. It encourages reading comprehension, observation, planning and problem-solving, while its rescue story gives players a personal reason to complete each objective.
Tools and technologies
We used C++17 for gameplay and simulation, SDL2 for the optional graphical interface, and a custom software renderer for terrain, robots, lighting, shadows and animated scenes. The project supports Make and CMake builds, with automated C++ tests covering mission progression, interactions and rescue sequences. Python and Pillow support preview generation.
Creativity and design considerations
The project combines scientific investigation with a rescue story told through a robot’s perspective. We considered clear objectives, readable inventory displays, consistent environments, retryable learning activities and reliable mission progression. We also documented where the fictional setting and simplified mechanics differ from real science.
